pages.text: Every morning, Philomena’s mother gave her five cedis for school. By the end of first break, it was gone. “Where does it all go?” she asked Elvis, as they stood at the tuck shop. Elvis opened his notebook. “Let us find out,” he said. “Today we write down every pesewa. I am the accountant, and you are the customer.”

I am the accountant, and you are the customer.”

pages.text: Madam Ocran’s stall was a wonderland: biscuits, groundnuts, bread, oranges, ice cream, fried yam and sachet water. Philomena bought a pack of biscuits, a juice, a bag of sweets and a plate of fried yam. “That was GH¢4.50 in ten minutes,” said Elvis, writing. “And then you shared nothing and had a tummy ache.” Philomena groaned. “It was delicious, though.”

pages.text: On Friday, Elvis showed her the week. “Monday, GH¢5. Tuesday, GH¢5. Wednesday, GH¢5. You spent GH¢25 on snacks, but only GH¢8 on food that fills you up. Ten per cent of your money went on sweets alone.” Philomena stared. “That is the price of not planning,” said Elvis. “A fool and his money are soon parted.” “Rude,” said Philomena, laughing.

pages.alt: A notebook with a table of daily spending and a small pie chart.

pages.text: They made a plan. Out of GH¢5, Philomena would spend GH¢2 on a proper snack, GH¢1 on water or fruit, GH¢1 to save, and GH¢1 to share or keep for emergencies. “That is the 2-1-1-1 rule,” said Elvis. “It is not magic, but it works. If you save GH¢1 a day for a school week, that is GH¢5.” Philomena wrote it on her palm in pen.

pages.text: On Monday, Philomena bought groundnuts and an orange. Madam Ocran smiled. “Good choice,” she said. “Groundnuts give you energy and protein, and the orange gives you vitamin C.” By Wednesday, Philomena was bargaining for an extra orange for her friend Elvis. By Friday, she had saved GH¢5. “I feel like a tycoon,” she said. “A small one,” said Elvis. “Do not break the bank.”

pages.text: With her saved GH¢5, Philomena did something surprising. She bought a small notebook for Lydia, a girl in her class who often had no pencil. “It is not charity,” she said. “It is a friend looking out for a friend.” Lydia was lost for words. Elvis nodded. “Saving is not only for you,” he whispered. “It is for sharing.”

pages.text: That evening, Philomena wrote to her Aunt Ewuraba. “Dear Aunt Ewuraba, I hope this letter finds you in good health. I am writing to tell you how I have changed the way I use my pocket money. I now plan my spending, I save a little each day, and I choose healthy snacks. Thank you for the advice you gave me at Christmas. Please say hello to everyone at home. Your loving niece, Philomena.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: in her letter, Philomena wrote full words, used a clear opening and kept every sentence complete. She did not write “tnx” for thank you or “pls” for please. She also gave details, which examiners like. Elvis read it and grinned. “You are not just a saver,” he said. “You are a writer.” The end.
